extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, federal judges, and litigation practitioners interested in separation-of-powers, judicial management, and enforcement-lawmaking litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Describes the forms of judicial case-management authority and doctrinal developments that judges use to force transparency, reason-giving, and adversarial testing in suits challenging executive enforcement actions. Explains specific managerial tools, examples, and doctrinal consequences for pre-enforcement review, standing, and remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges have considerable authority over the timing of suit, which has a transparency-forcing function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Through case management judges can speed disposition (e.g., proceed to judgment without certain depositions) to obtain a fully reasoned opinion earlier and thereby change the posture of appellate review or force the Executive to commit publicly to reasons. Example: district court in the census litigation proceeded to judgment without Secretary Ross's deposition, producing a reasoned opinion before the Supreme Court heard discovery issues and thereby forcing public commitment on the merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holding Conferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges may hale parties into informal conferences where they can check in with and question parties outside formal oral argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informal conferences give judges an opportunity to question government representatives and probe public statements or legal positions (e.g., DACA-related questioning of a DHS Secretary's public statement). Resnik is cited emphasizing the authority judges exercise in these settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial Notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts can take judicial notice of adjudicative facts not subject to reasonable dispute, including events or statements outside the formal record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Federal Rule of Evidence 201, courts often take formal and informal notice of widely known external facts (e.g., presidential announcements, tweets, public speeches), expanding the judicial record and bringing executive action under earlier supervision. Examples: Sierra Club v. Trump (taking note of a presidential speech); Dep’t of Commerce quotation about ordinary-citizen knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amicus Participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts can shape issues and arguments by managing amicus participation, including permitting 'litigating amici' that participate broadly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges have discretion over whether and how to address amici arguments in opinions and can allow amici to broaden the scope of issues in a suit; amici—particularly congressional amici—can introduce arguments that change litigation dynamics. The text notes courts can choose how much to address amici and that Part III explores effects when suits challenge enforcement lawmaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorney Withdrawals
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts can scrutinize and manage government attorney withdrawal motions to force accountability and reason-giving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although withdrawals are routinely granted, courts may require reasons or assurances when government lawyers seek to withdraw, use local rules or their discretion to demand explanations about inconsistencies, and deny or condition withdrawals to ensure continuity and public accountability. Examples: S.D.N.Y. denied substitution absent 'satisfactory reasons'; District of Maryland required assurances re conflicts and denied without prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-trial Management
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-trial remedies (especially injunctive orders) allow courts to continue oversight of executive action after judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permanent injunctions often contemplate ongoing judicial supervision and retention of jurisdiction to enforce remedy terms (e.g., New York v. U.S. Dep’t of Commerce retaining jurisdiction until census results processed). Post-trial management injects courts into administration of remedies and can sustain transparency and compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-ordered disclosure and inquiry into executive misstatements
rubrics_metrics.description: A court can order defendants to file comprehensive, detailed reports listing inaccurate or misleading statements, identify responsible actors, and describe who/when/how inaccuracies were discovered; the court may retain jurisdiction to pursue inquiry even if suit is mooted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Managerial orders of this sort do not necessarily fall under discovery powers but under broader case-management authority; example: Wolf litigation where judge ordered a detailed report and retained jurisdiction to investigate misstatements after public admissions and the U.S. Attorney’s Office letter acknowledging inaccuracies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intervention by non-party institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts can permit intervention by other governmental or institutional actors to ensure adversarial defense of legislative or other interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intervention can introduce vigorous advocacy for positions the Executive refuses to defend (e.g., BLAG's intervention in Windsor to defend Congress's statute), thereby forcing public reasons and pushing back against Executive control of litigation participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment: managing criminal contempt (special prosecutor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may appoint a special prosecutor or counsel to represent a position abandoned by the United States or when the government declines to prosecute contempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 42(a)(2) mandates requesting a government attorney to prosecute contempt and permits appointment of another if the government declines; Ninth Circuit in United States v. Arpaio appointed a special prosecutor on appeal, keeping the case live and forcing DOJ to publicly respond. The court relied on FRCP 42 and inherent authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment: protecting integrity of the judicial forum (amicus appointment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts can appoint an amicus curiae to present arguments opposing government motions or to address concerns about the integrity of proceedings (e.g., potential perjury or irregular plea-posture issues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts may use inherent authority to appoint an amicus to ensure adversarial briefing and institutional protections (example: District of D.C. appointed amicus to oppose DOJ's motion to dismiss in Flynn and to address whether contempt proceedings were warranted); appellate courts may review such appointments (Flynn produced mandamus and en banc proceedings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Managerial authority as a tool to force transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges' managerial discretion — though potentially evading structural checks — can be used to force reason-giving and transparency on the Executive branch in public-law litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Managerial judging draws public scrutiny, lessening concerns about unchecked decisions; appellate review remains available. The piece notes managerial authority can compel public commitments, produce disclosures, and bring suits earlier, expanding judicial supervision. It also warns of risks of judicial overreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relaxed ripeness and pre-enforcement review for enforcement lawmaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have regularly entertained pre-enforcement challenges to enforcement lawmaking by relaxing ripeness/imminence barriers when the Executive's enforcement posture fixes legal obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three doctrinal effects: (1) ripeness/imminence is often satisfied in enforcement-lawmaking suits; (2) courts interpret enforcement laws during the pre-merits ripeness stage, elevating legal questions; (3) courts take judicial notice of unconventional external sources in this context. Example: Northern District of Texas rejecting DOE’s ripeness argument in transgender student Title IX challenge; references to Abbott Laboratories and Clapper doctrinal context.
